title: Buying a cornet at 16, first parade, and first jobs after the break
summary: Visits to Manuel Perez's lessons made him want cornet. He bought one at 16, played a 1926 carnival parade, quit for about three years, then in 1928 took a first job with a Barbarin brother's band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Getting my first drums, with or without lessons

blocks.x: I don't exactly know if she would have been, although Manuel did pass away around 42, 43. I'm not sure what year, but I was somewhere, and I was in the Army, I think it was. Anyhow, and what made me like trumpet or cornet so much is because my mother used to take me there lots of time, visiting when I was a kid. And he was giving lessons, and I just took to the trumpet or cornet. And I always didn't want to play a cornet. So, like I said, she wanted me to play violin, but I didn't like violin. So I went until right after, just right after one, especially, I mean exactly one week rather, after my 16th birthday, I had saved some money. I had a newspaper route, and I used to work in between school vacations. So I just saved that money, and I bought myself a little cornet. It was a little short one. It was a con wonder with a tuning device in the rear. And from then, well, I've started ever since then. And by coincidence, after learning, I learned about six, seven pieces. I hadn't taken any lessons, but I learned about six, seven pieces, and I played a job. That was the carnival day right after that. That was in 1926. It was a dance job or parade? No, it was a parade, in a street parade, on the carnival day. Then I began taking lessons with Manuel Perez. He was my first teacher. Then I sort of got discouraged like kids do, and I put the horn down. I left the horn down for about two and a half to three years. I didn't touch the horn anymore. Then I picked it back up, I'd say around 28 or the latter part of 28. And that's when I started playing. My first job was with Paul Barbaran's youngest brother. He was a drummer. You know, there were three drummers. Lewis, Charles, I can't call his name, the name was the banjo player. We used to call him Fushnik. Everybody around New Orleans knew Fushnik. Well, he left. He went to Chicago years ago. He was a banjo player. And Edgar Saussure was the clarinet, rather the saxophone player. Oh no.
Well, this is Saussure I knew in Chicago, played, Lee Collins played drums. Is that right?

Well this is Edgar Saussure, he's my wife's first cousin. He's in Frisco today. There must be some relative of that. Undoubtedly he is. But anyhow he played saxophone with us.
